# The Line

For eleven months after my father died, I kept paying his phone bill.

It was forty-two dollars a month, which is not nothing, but it is less than I spent on the therapist who suggested, gently and more than once, that I cancel it. I told her I was still sorting out his accounts. This was true in the way that most of what I told her was true: technically, and with a lot of furniture moved in front of it.

The real reason was the greeting. My father recorded it in 2009, when he first got a cell phone. He'd resisted for years, calling them leashes, and when he finally relented he treated the phone like a guest who might steal something. The greeting was eight seconds long. *This is Walter. I'm not near the phone, or I'm near it and ignoring it. Leave a message and I'll consider it.*

He thought that was hilarious. He'd make people call him just so they could hear it.

I called it maybe twice a week. Sometimes more. I never left a message. I'd listen to his voice, the slight rasp he got in the afternoons, the little catch before *consider*, as if he were trying not to laugh at his own joke, and then I'd hang up before the beep. It felt important not to leave a message. A message would be an admission that no one was going to consider it.

I also had the password to his voicemail, because I had set it up for him, because he was my father and I was the one who set things up. At first I didn't check it. Then, around the third month, I did.

There were forty-one messages. Most were from people who hadn't heard. A dentist's office. A man named Gary who wanted to know if Walt was still coming to the thing on Saturday. My aunt, twice, before I'd called her. A robotic voice warning him that his car's extended warranty was about to expire, which it had, along with everything else.

I deleted Gary after listening to it six times. I don't know why that one hurt most. Maybe because the thing on Saturday sounded fun, and my father had not told me about it, and now I'd never know what it was. He had a life that I was only now discovering was larger than the part of it that faced me.

After that I checked every week. It became a kind of ritual, like watering a plant in a house where no one lives. The messages thinned out. People learned. By month six, it was almost entirely spam: a woman offering to lower his interest rate, a man in a hurry about his Social Security number, an occasional silence followed by a click. I listened to all of them. I began to feel oddly tender toward the spam callers. They were the only ones who still believed he was out there. They were loyal in their way.

In the ninth month, there was a message from a stranger.

"Hi, uh, this is for Walter Brennan. Mr. Brennan, you won't remember me. My name's Denise Alvarado. I'm calling because—okay, this is going to sound strange."

She paused. I could hear traffic behind her, a turn signal ticking.

"In 1994 you were driving on Route 9 near the reservoir and you stopped for a car in a ditch. That was me. I was nineteen and I'd been drinking, which I've never told anybody, and you didn't call the police. You pulled me out and you drove me home and you made me promise I'd never do it again. And I didn't. I haven't had a drink in thirty years. I'm a nurse now. I have two kids. My oldest just turned nineteen, and I keep thinking about how close I came, and I realized I never thanked you. I found your name on an old receipt, you gave me your number in case my parents wanted to talk to you, and I kept it. I don't know why I kept it. Anyway. Thank you. That's all. You probably don't even remember."

She left her number.

I listened to it on my kitchen floor, which is where I apparently sit now when the ground moves. I listened to it again. My father had never mentioned this. Not once, in thirty years of telling the same six stories at every Thanksgiving, the one about the goat, the one about the flooded basement in '78, had he said anything about pulling a girl out of a ditch.

I tried to think why. Maybe he'd forgotten. Maybe it seemed ordinary to him. Or maybe, and this felt most like him, he'd simply decided it was her story and not his.

It took me four days to call her back. When I told her, she was quiet for a long time, and then she said, "Oh," in a way that contained a whole second conversation. We talked for an hour. She told me what he'd been wearing, a green Carhartt jacket I remembered, that I'd thrown into a donation bin in month two and had regretted ever since. She said he'd sung along to the radio on the drive, badly. That he'd told her she was going to be fine, and said it like it was an instruction.

"He was right," she said. "I just wanted him to know."

"I think he knew," I said, though I didn't know if that was true. Then I said, "Actually, I think he considered it."

She didn't get the joke. There was no way she could have. I didn't explain.

I canceled the line in the eleventh month. Before I did, I called it one last time and, for the first time, I stayed on past the beep.

I didn't say much. I told him about Denise. I told him about the jacket. I told him I was sorry I'd never asked for more of his stories, the ones that weren't about goats.

Then I said, "That's all," and hung up, and let someone else consider it.
